When the Iroquois League formed
column2: In the late 1500s five nations, the Mohawks, Oneidas, Onondagas, Cayugas and Senecas, formed the Iroquois League confederacy.

column1: When Cartier first sailed to Canada
column2: In 1535 Jacques Cartier made the first official French voyage to Canada, through the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

column1: When France founded its first permanent colony
column2: In 1605 the French founded Port Royal in Acadia (Nova Scotia), their first permanent colony in North America.

column1: When Champlain founded Quebec
column2: In 1608, three years after Port Royal, Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec up the St. Lawrence to trade furs with less European competition.

column1: When Champlain shot the Mohawk chiefs
column2: In 1609 Champlain shot dead two Mohawk chiefs in what is now upstate New York, letting his Indian allies drive off 200 Mohawk warriors.

column1: When Henry Hudson explored the Hudson River
column2: In 1609 the Englishman Henry Hudson explored the Hudson River for the Dutch, giving them their claim there.

column1: How much a beaver hat cost in the 1610s
column2: As early as the 1610s a beaver hat sold for ten times the price of a wool hat, because Europeans had trapped their own beavers nearly to extinction.

column1: When the Dutch founded New Netherland
column2: In 1624 the Dutch founded New Netherland around the Hudson, Connecticut and Delaware Rivers.

column1: When the Mohawks took over the Fort Orange trade
column2: By 1630 the Mohawks had pushed aside rivals and dominated the Dutch fur trade at Fort Orange.

column1: How many Hurons smallpox killed, 1634 to 1640
column2: From 1634 to 1640 smallpox killed more than 10,000 Hurons, cutting their population in half.

column1: When the Iroquois destroyed the Hurons
column2: In 1648 and 1649 well-armed Iroquois warriors destroyed Huron towns, and the Hurons burned their remaining towns and abandoned their homeland for good.

column1: When the Beaver Wars began
column2: The Beaver Wars began in the 1640s and went on in fits and starts for the rest of the 1600s.

column1: How the Beaver Wars hurt New France by 1666
column2: About 300 Frenchmen were killed or captured in the Beaver Wars, cutting New France's small population in half by 1666.

column1: When La Salle reached the mouth of the Mississippi
column2: In 1682 La Salle became the first European to travel down the Mississippi to its mouth at the Gulf of Mexico.

column1: How big New France was in 1700
column2: In 1700 New France had about 15,000 people, three modest towns (Quebec, Montreal and Trois-Rivières) and scores of simple missions.

column1: When James I became king
column2: In 1603 James I succeeded Elizabeth I and vowed to purge England of Puritan reformers.

column1: When the Separatists moved to Holland
column2: By 1608 some English Separatists had moved to Holland for its complete religious freedom.

column1: When epidemic devastated coastal New England
column2: From 1616 to 1618 a massive epidemic struck coastal New England, cutting the native population by as much as 90 percent.

column1: When and how many Pilgrims landed at Plymouth
column2: In November 1620 about 88 Separatist Pilgrims anchored at Plymouth, sick with scurvy and weak from malnutrition.

column1: How many Pilgrims died by spring 1621
column2: By spring 1621 half of the Plymouth immigrants had died, because they arrived too late to plant and lacked food.

column1: When the Pilgrims held their harvest feast
column2: In 1621 the Pilgrims invited Wampanoag leaders to a feast for their first successful harvest, the origin of the "First Thanksgiving" story.

column1: When Charles I dissolved Parliament
column2: In 1629 Charles I dissolved Parliament and ruled without it, then moved against the Puritans.

column1: When the Massachusetts Bay Company was organized
column2: In 1629 Puritan merchants, gentlemen and lawyers organized the Massachusetts Bay Company, and advance parties founded Salem.

column1: When Winthrop founded Boston
column2: In 1630 John Winthrop's fleet arrived in Massachusetts Bay and founded Boston.

column1: When church members became freemen in Massachusetts
column2: In 1631 Massachusetts Bay made every adult male church member a freeman with the vote.

column1: How many came in the Great Migration
column2: About 21,000 Puritan immigrants came to New England between 1630 and 1642, until the English Civil War cut off arrivals.

column1: How long first-generation New Englanders lived
column2: First-generation New Englanders lived to an average age of 70, nearly twice as long as Virginians and ten years longer than people in England.

column1: How many New England children survived
column2: About 90 percent of New England children reached adulthood, and a typical family raised seven or eight children to maturity.

column1: How fast New England's population doubled
column2: New England's population doubled about every 27 years through natural increase, while Europe and the Chesapeake barely reproduced themselves.

column1: How many people New England and the Chesapeake had in 1700
column2: By 1700 New England and the Chesapeake each had about 100,000 people, but New England grew by natural increase and the Chesapeake by importing servants.

column1: How much land a New England family received
column2: Each New England family received a house lot and about 150 acres in nearby fields, leaving much uncultivated for future generations.

column1: When Hooker founded Connecticut
column2: In 1636 Thomas Hooker led part of his Cambridge congregation to Connecticut, the first English settlement there.

column1: When Roger Williams founded Providence
column2: In 1636 Roger Williams, fleeing deportation, founded Providence, later part of Rhode Island.

column1: When Anne Hutchinson was expelled
column2: In 1638 Massachusetts Bay expelled Anne Hutchinson and her followers for sedition.

column1: When the Pequot War was fought
column2: In 1637 colonists and Narragansett allies fought the Pequot War, burning the main Pequot village and killing hundreds.

column1: How many Algonquins lived in New England at contact
column2: About 100,000 Algonquin people lived from the Kennebec River in Maine to Cape Cod when the English arrived.

column1: How many New Englanders were charged with witchcraft
column2: In the first colonial century 344 New Englanders were charged with witchcraft, and more than three-quarters of them were women.

column1: When the Salem witch trials took place
column2: In 1692 the Salem witchcraft trials led to twenty executions before Increase Mather and fourteen other ministers warned against them.

column1: When John Eliot began preaching to the Indians
column2: In the 1640s John Eliot began preaching in Algonquian, and he later set up seven praying towns for Christian Indians.

column1: When Metacom's War was fought
column2: Metacom's War (King Philip's War) was fought in 1675 and 1676, ending with Metacom's death in the summer of 1676.

column1: How close Metacom's warriors came to Boston
column2: By spring 1676 Metacom's warriors had wasted more than two dozen Plymouth Colony towns and were raiding within 20 miles of Boston.

column1: How deadly Metacom's War was
column2: In proportion to population, Metacom's War caused twice the casualties for New England that the whole United States later suffered in the Civil War.

column1: When the Dutch West India Company went bankrupt
column2: In 1654 the Dutch West India Company went bankrupt and virtually abandoned New Netherland.

column1: When the English took New Netherland
column2: In 1664 the Duke of York's invading fleet made the Dutch surrender New Netherland, which became New York.

column1: How many colonists New York had in 1664 and 1698
column2: The Duke of York inherited about 9,000 colonists in 1664, but political strife kept New York to only 18,000 people by 1698.

column1: When New Jersey was founded
column2: In 1664 the Duke of York gave about 5 million acres between the Hudson and Delaware Rivers to Berkeley and Carteret, founding New Jersey.

column1: When New Jersey became a royal colony
column2: In 1702 the Crown reunited East and West Jersey as one royal colony.

column1: How many Quakers England had by 1660
column2: By 1660 about 40,000 English merchants, artisans and farmers were Quakers, and many suffered fines, prison and beatings.

column1: When William Penn received Pennsylvania
column2: In 1681 Charles II granted William Penn all the land between New Jersey and Maryland.

column1: When Penn annexed Delaware
column2: In 1682 Penn bought and annexed the Three Lower Counties (later Delaware), home to about 1,000 Dutch, Swedes and Finns.

column1: How many people Pennsylvania had by 1700
column2: By 1700 Pennsylvania had about 21,000 people, a migration matched in size only by Puritan New England.

column1: What share of Pennsylvania settlers were servants
column2: About half of Pennsylvania's settlers were indentured servants, and the rest were families of free farmers and artisans.

column1: When Pennsylvania adopted the Charter of Privileges
column2: In 1701 Penn's Charter of Privileges took lawmaking power from the council and left the elected one-house assembly in control.

column1: When Parliament passed the first Navigation Act
column2: In 1651 Parliament passed the first Navigation Act; before it England had no coherent policy for regulating colonial trade.

column1: When the Dominion of New England was created
column2: In 1686 the Lords of Trade combined the New England colonies under a royal governor, and in 1688 they added New York and New Jersey.

column1: When the Glorious Revolution happened
column2: In 1688 Parliament forced James II into exile and made William and Mary monarchs in the Glorious Revolution.

column1: When Massachusetts got its new charter
column2: In 1691 Massachusetts received a new charter making it a royal colony, joined with Plymouth and Maine.

column1: When England tightened colonial trade enforcement
column2: In 1696 Parliament added customs officials and vice-admiralty courts in the colonies, and the king created the Board of Trade.

column1: Which colonies were royal by 1700
column2: By 1700 Virginia, New York, Massachusetts and New Hampshire had royal governments, with New Jersey, the Carolinas and Georgia soon to follow.

column1: How many British, French and Spanish colonists there were in 1720
column2: In 1720 the British had nearly 400,000 colonists, the French about 25,000 and the Spanish about 5,000, yet Indians still controlled over 90 percent of the land.

column1: How often Louis XIV went to war
column2: Louis XIV sent France's army against its neighbors four times between 1667 and 1714.
